What do the Olympic rings and their colours mean?

The Olympic rings represent unity, but their colours do not label individual continents. Discover the flag-colour story behind the familiar symbol.

By Biel Sardà · Published 29 Sept 2026 · Suggest a correction

What do the five rings represent?

The five Olympic rings represent the union of five continents and athletes meeting from around the world. The symbol works as a whole: there is no official rule assigning one ring colour to each continent.

That second point is the quiz trap. A neat colour-coded map is easy to remember, which does not make it the official explanation. The International Olympic Committee’s answer explicitly rejects that colour-to-continent match.

Five rings, rather than five labels

Think of the linked rings as a picture of people coming together. Separating the colours into a list of continent labels misses the point of the interlocking design.

It is a useful habit for any symbol question: check whether the meaning belongs to the whole design or to each piece individually.

Why these colours?

Pierre de Coubertin created the rings in 1913. The IOC explains that blue, yellow, black, green and red, together with the white background, represented the colours found in national flags at the time.

White is easy to forget because it sits behind the rings. The background still belongs to the story.

The answer to keep in your pocket

If a friend asks which continent the blue ring stands for, the helpful answer is: none is officially assigned to it. The five rings together express unity.

One way to remember the distinction: linked rings bring athletes together; coloured labels would split them apart. It is a memory cue, not a new official meaning.
